The thing is that a big part of Linux (and Unix in general), is the philosophy that everything should do one thing, and do it well. Systemd goes very far in the opposite direction; it tries to be one thing which manages everything from booting the system to wifi to login and more. Some widespread systems, like the Gnome desktop environment, has also started to depend on systemd, not working at all if you want to use something else than systemd. To a lot of people, it seems really crazy that a desktop environment should have a hard dependency on an init system; those two seem like they really shouldn't have anything to do with each other. There are also some controversian technical decisions, like making log files some weird binary format instead of plaintext, forcing you to use a specific tool to read them instead of being able to use any of the great tools available which works on text. A binary format also means that in the case of corruption, you could end up with a completely unreadable file, instead of just losing a section of it.

Note to pro-systemd people: I know the arguments against what I listed; systemd is multiple binaries and could therefore be considered to not technically be the same thing, you could use gnome on non-systemd systems by running various systemd shims, and there are already things, like X, which don't follow the unix philosophy. I'm just trying to give an outline as to what the controversy is about.

and in the other corner:

In this case, however, it's the init system (and quite a bit more) that's being evolved.

systemd

systemd is a very different approach to how Linux systems have traditionally been handled. In that many parts other than 'init' have been overhauled/absorbed as well. To allow for things like activation on device states, fs changes, or dbus registration, all of those sub-systems have started migrating under the "systemd umbrella".

The results benefit distros and developers alike because "it just works" and brings the maintenance cost and barrier to entry down; thus adoption has been quick (relatively). For better or worse, it happened quicker than many people are comfortable with. Add on to that the obsoleting of all the old init/service scripts in favor of a newly-defined config format and it's no wonder red flags go up.

"Everything was working just fine, and now I have to re-learn everything." --lots of people

Another debatable issue is the logging in systemd (aka journald). Going from text files to binary logs allowed embedding metadata as well as verifiable logs. But the ecosystem of tools for text-based logs is left behind and many things need to be extended/rebuilt that have existed successfully for a long time. For someone with a system that doesn't need to change, (read: isn't broken) re-investing in all new tools doesn't make much sense; especially if you want to validate everything you're installing. On the other hand you have a very consistent way to access log data from all services with, again, a lower barrier to entry.

There is also the issue of portability. systemd is specifically a linux technology. So anything that depends on it, or targets it, kind of implicitly targets linux and leaves out other systems.

Below here lies my own opinion on systemd, but isn't really a response to the OP's question and can be safely ignored

IMO there is a lot of FUD. And from my perspective, the majority (nearly all?) of the anti-systemd points I've read don't make actual cases/points, but instead refer to "unix philosophy", "monolithic (like the kernel)", conspiracy or the inverse of NIH (it's all invented over there). That is to say: I don't see cases against new devs or productivity. For example, GNOME's dependency: the current systems were severely lacking, and the first real solution to market gets sucked up by those that would spend their time solving other problems.

I like to imagine that there are still communities that can have technical discussions without it needlessly devolving into a religious debate. I have been far more productive working with systemd than in any other init system, especially when it comes to on-boarding new devs/admins. So to do my part here are my cases:

systemd suites my own needs very well because:

As someone who builds tools/services:

  • my .service file works on all distros and didn't take me any meaningful time to write out
  • i get strong guarantees around env, logging, resources, and dependencies
  • i spend more time developing my app rather than defensive init scripts
  • nobody else is going to maintain an init script for me
  • I'm guaranteed consistency when activating (if it works once, it always works)

As someone who manages services/servers:

  • one place to manage all of my logs, without micro-managing configs
  • cross distro service commands
  • simple run on startup (enable/disable)
  • consistency means better tools, and less debugging
  • context, environment, network, user, etc.. not a problem
  • straight forward to export all logs to ELK/Splunk/Graylog
  • universal log size/history management
  • stdout is a universal interface, if you print it, it gets logged (by default)
  • if a service spawns 100 workers, I can manage the entire group with no effort (e.g. httpd)

As an everyday desktop user:

  • when something weird happens with the nvidia driver, i can see all of the session logs without digging (journalctl --user)
  • if i need to restart gdm, or otherwise my session, because of my nvidia driver, cgroups make cleanup easy
  • when I start steam, I can have it mount an external drive to my library on disk access
  • networkd is ridiculously fast at getting a connection up
  • custom services are portable
  • don't have to learn each distro's init system
  • no more reverse engineering init scripts

Technically you can do anything with anything. But having an idea doesn't make it practical, a good idea, teachable or maintainable.

You can technically make a shell script to start a service in a control group, with the right user, with its own context/temp directory, that automatically restarts, and checks for a dead PID file and some fancy work to prevent the edge-case race conditions. But you could also write a few lines of configuration to say you want those things explicitly and do something else. You know-for-a-fact it will work, and others can understand it with limited/no knowledge of the service. Put another way: by now it's possible to observe what init scripts are used for and design something to accomplish that in a standard way.

I mean come-on, I can walk through a systemd unit file and my GF can understand what's happening. if you're reading this, I meant nothing by that, it is just an example since you've just started learning the command line :D

Also, a systemd unit file is a defined space, with defined actions/settings. It is not a shell script and there's ample documentation on what does what. So, therefore, it should be trivial to take a .service file and generate a script from it for your os/distro of choice. Grab a .service file, and generate your flavor of init script. In fact, a non-systemd distro could then use any .service file config with little effort. That gives us a single source of truth, to generate init scripts for any system, and in an automated way. People that don't know YOUR init system can make a .service file that does the right things for their app, and you have a standard way to interpret it.

If everyone has to start at square one, everyone will waste time. Distros have included helper scripts with their init system for consistency and to keep things stable. systemd is a massive evolution of that concept. Massive may not be a big-enough term.. but you get the idea. I think many of the ideas in systemd are what most of us would actually come up with if we sat down, had a real technical discussion, and tried to solve those problems. How do we commoditize service setup? How do we prevent log spoofing between services? How do we guarantee log files have not been tampered with? etc..
